title: Roots Hold the Soil: Parent Guide
endLine: Roots and leaves hold soil in place when rain falls.

scenes.tts: After a storm, a stream can run brown with mud. Where does that mud come from? Two trays of soil and a watering can will show you.
scenes.caption: After a storm, a stream can run brown with mud. Where does that mud come from? Two trays of soil and a watering can will show you.
scenes.visual: A friendly schematic landscape: a gentle green hill on the left, a bare brown patch on the right, and a stream at the bottom running brown with swirls of mud. Soft rain lines fall and fade. Large text appears: 'Where does the mud come from?' No photos of real children.
scenes.narration: After a storm, a stream can run brown with mud. Where does that mud come from? Two trays of soil and a watering can will show you.

scenes.visual: Same landscape stays in place; the rain stops. Title 'Roots Hold the Soil' appears at top left for 2 seconds while the brown stream keeps flowing slowly.

scenes.tts: Once the trays are ready, the test takes about thirty-five minutes. Your child makes a guess and compares the cups after giving both trays the same rain. They practice explaining what the cups show.
scenes.caption: Once the trays are ready, the test takes about thirty-five minutes. Your child makes a guess and compares the cups after giving both trays the same rain. They practice explaining what the cups show.
scenes.visual: The landscape slides back; on a simple table in front, two matching cartons lie on their sides with a clear cup in front of each. Three labels appear one by one beside them: 'Make a guess', 'Same rain on both', 'Cups check it'.
scenes.narration: Once the trays are ready, the test takes about thirty-five minutes. Your child makes a guess and compares the cups after giving both trays the same rain. They practice explaining what the cups show.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child throughout. Use bagged soil and plain, untreated seed. Sow it thickly in one tray two to three weeks ahead. Keep it moist in a sunny spot. Or press sod into the tray that day.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child throughout. Use bagged soil and plain, untreated seed. Sow it thickly in one tray two to three weeks ahead. Keep it moist in a sunny spot. Or press sod into the tray that day.
scenes.visual: On the same table, an adult opens a bag of soil outdoors. Untreated seed drops onto damp soil in one tray. Show a sunny spot and the calendar turning. Then show the same tray with a piece of sod as the quick option.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child throughout. Use bagged soil and plain, untreated seed. Sow it thickly in one tray two to three weeks ahead. Keep it moist in a sunny spot. Or press sod into the tray that day.

scenes.tts: Fill the bare tray with bagged soil about five centimeters deep. If you grew grass from seed, use the same bagged soil in both trays. You cut a small notch at the low end of each. Raise the other ends on books, to the same height. Set a clear plastic cup under each notch.
scenes.caption: Fill the bare tray with bagged soil about five centimeters deep. If you grew grass from seed, use the same bagged soil in both trays. You cut a small notch at the low end of each. Raise the other ends on books, to the same height. Set a clear plastic cup under each notch.
scenes.visual: The second carton fills with bare soil to a marked line '5 cm'. An adult's hand with scissors snips a small V notch at one end of each carton (adult hand only). Stacks of books slide under the far ends so both tilt equally; clear plastic cups slide under the notches at the table edge.
scenes.narration: Fill the bare tray with bagged soil about five centimeters deep. If you grew grass from seed, use the same bagged soil in both trays. You cut a small notch at the low end of each. Raise the other ends on books, to the same height. Set a clear plastic cup under each notch.

scenes.tts: Give both trays the same slope and the same rain. One tray is bare, and the other has grass. Ask your child, 'Which cup will get more mud?' Write the guess down before you pour.
scenes.caption: Give both trays the same slope and the same rain. One tray is bare, and the other has grass. Ask your child, 'Which cup will get more mud?' Write the guess down before you pour.
scenes.visual: Show the matching slopes and highlight the grass on one tray. Show the question 'Which cup gets muddier?' Then show the adult writing the child's guess without revealing the result.
scenes.narration: Give both trays the same slope and the same rain. One tray is bare, and the other has grass. Ask your child, 'Which cup will get more mud?' Write the guess down before you pour.

scenes.tts: For gentle rain, hold the watering can about twenty centimeters above the high end. Pour two cups over about thirty seconds. Repeat with the same amount, height, and speed. What do you predict the cups will look like?
scenes.caption: For gentle rain, hold the watering can about twenty centimeters above the high end. Pour two cups over about thirty seconds. Repeat with the same amount, height, and speed. What do you predict the cups will look like?
scenes.visual: Show the can hovering above the high end of the bare tray. Show the pour height and duration with simple labels. Highlight both trays in turn, with both catch cups empty. Keep the prediction question on screen.
scenes.narration: For gentle rain, hold the watering can about twenty centimeters above the high end. Pour two cups over about thirty seconds. Repeat with the same amount, height, and speed. What do you predict the cups will look like?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card and both empty catch cups on screen for the pause. The can hovers above the high end of the bare tray. Let the grass blades sway slightly.

scenes.tts: The bare tray's runoff is usually cloudier. The grass tray's cup often has less water. Ask, 'Where did the soil in this cup come from?' Check the guess. After ten minutes, measure the settled soil with a ruler.
scenes.caption: The bare tray's runoff is usually cloudier. The grass tray's cup often has less water. Ask, 'Where did the soil in this cup come from?' Check the guess. After ten minutes, measure the settled soil with a ruler.
scenes.visual: Pour onto both trays in turn, with the same height and timing, and reveal the cups. Show the bare cup usually cloudier and the grass cup usually clearer. Bring back the guess sheet. Advance a schematic clock ten minutes and show the ruler against the settled layers.
scenes.narration: The bare tray's runoff is usually cloudier. The grass tray's cup often has less water. Ask, 'Where did the soil in this cup come from?' Check the guess. After ten minutes, measure the settled soil with a ruler.

scenes.tts: Empty the cups. Pour two fresh cups onto each tray, taking about five seconds per tray. Look for small channels called rills. After ten minutes, measure the settled soil again. Lift the grass with a spoon to see the roots.
scenes.caption: Empty the cups. Pour two fresh cups onto each tray, taking about five seconds per tray. Look for small channels called rills. After ten minutes, measure the settled soil again. Lift the grass with a spoon to see the roots.
scenes.visual: Show both catch cups emptied. Measure and pour fresh water onto each tray in turn at the same faster rate. Highlight any rills on the bare soil. Advance the schematic clock ten minutes and measure the settled layers. Lift one grass edge with a spoon to show roots gripping soil.
scenes.narration: Empty the cups. Pour two fresh cups onto each tray, taking about five seconds per tray. Look for small channels called rills. After ten minutes, measure the settled soil again. Lift the grass with a spoon to see the roots.

scenes.tts: Leaves and stems soften the impact of falling drops. Roots grip the soil and help water soak in. On bare soil, raindrops can knock grains loose. Water flowing downhill can carry those grains into the cup.
scenes.caption: Leaves and stems soften the impact of falling drops. Roots grip the soil and help water soak in. On bare soil, raindrops can knock grains loose. Water flowing downhill can carry those grains into the cup.
scenes.visual: A simple cross-section of the two trays side by side. On the grass side, drops land on blades and slide down gently; roots spread below and blue arrows show water soaking in. On the bare side, drops hit the soil and splash grains up, which ride away downhill. Labels: 'Leaves soften drops', 'Roots grip'.
scenes.narration: Leaves and stems soften the impact of falling drops. Roots grip the soil and help water soak in. On bare soil, raindrops can knock grains loose. Water flowing downhill can carry those grains into the cup.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child. You do the cutting and lift the wet trays. Keep small pieces and seed away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Never taste plants, soil, or seed. Wash hands with soap and water afterward.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child. You do the cutting and lift the wet trays. Keep small pieces and seed away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Never taste plants, soil, or seed. Wash hands with soap and water afterward.
scenes.visual: Show an adult trimming a tray and folding or taping a foil edge, then lifting a wet tray. Show the seed packet out of reach with the label 'Under 4: choking risk' and then 'Call 911 if choking'. End at a handwashing sink.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child. You do the cutting and lift the wet trays. Keep small pieces and seed away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Never taste plants, soil, or seed. Wash hands with soap and water afterward.

scenes.tts: For an optional walk, check the weather and choose shade or use sun protection. Wait until rain stops and at least thirty minutes after the last thunder. Stay together on a dry path where you have permission. Stay away from roads, storm drains, steep crumbling banks, and bodies of water. Never walk through floodwater. At a bare patch, ask, 'How could we fix it?' Check for ticks afterward. Wash hands with soap and water after handling soil or plants.

scenes.visual: Return to the opening landscape. Show the adult and child on a dry path away from water and drains. At a bare patch, show three sketches of possible fixes: grass, mulch, and leaves. The sketches stay on the plan next to the patch.

scenes.visual: End card over a close-up of rain hitting the grass tray and roots gripping its soil. Large centered text: 'Roots and leaves hold soil in place when rain falls.'
